\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We tested whether SDF supervision and collision-aware evaluation deliver reliable geometric safety for VLAs. Action collapse renders reported CAR illusory; dfCAR corrects this using only EE position logging (\S\ref{sec:dfcar}). EE-only oracle SDF refinement is counterproductive, reducing CAR by 5--10\,pp as unmonitored links rotate through obstacles (\S\ref{sec:ee_only}), and collision-free demonstrations account for nearly all avoidance gains with no statistically significant SDF benefit (\S\ref{sec:avoidance_source}). More broadly, dfCAR provides a lightweight diagnostic that any VLA pipeline can adopt to screen for action-collapse contamination, and point-supervision of a single link is insufficient for articulated robots; genuine geometric safety will require full-body collision representations and cross-architecture validation.

3	We tested whether SDF supervision and collision-aware evaluation deliver reliable geometric safety for VLAs. More broadly, dfCAR provides a lightweight diagnostic that any VLA pipeline can adopt to screen for action-collapse contamination, and point-supervision of a single link is insufficient for articulated robots; genuine geometric safety will require full-body collision representations and cross-architecture validation.
4	
5	\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limitations}
6	
7	All experiments use MuJoCo simulation (SafeLIBERO, two VLA families, four pick-and-place tasks); action collapse is structurally general but untested on other benchmarks or real hardware. dfCAR assumes bimodal displacement separation (Figure~\ref{fig:displacement}), which may require task-specific calibration when less pronounced. The EE-only SDF null result is specific to auxiliary loss integration and should not be extrapolated to constrained optimization or runtime filtering (Section~\ref{sec:related}). Oracle refinement uses a single seed per variant ($n{=}1$, 160 episodes). The training ablation ($n{=}3$ seeds; MDE ${\approx}$ 5.6\,pp at 80\% power) cannot rule out a small SDF effect (2--5\,pp) without larger samples.

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We tested whether SDF supervision and collision-aware evaluation deliver reliable geometric safety for VLAs. Action collapse renders reported CAR illusory; dfCAR corrects this using only EE position logging (\S\ref{sec:dfcar}). EE-only oracle SDF refinement is counterproductive, reducing CAR by 5--10\,pp as unmonitored links rotate through obstacles (\S\ref{sec:ee_only}), and collision-free demonstrations account for nearly all avoidance gains with no statistically significant SDF benefit (\S\ref{sec:avoidance_source}). More broadly, dfCAR provides a lightweight diagnostic that any VLA pipeline can adopt to screen for action-collapse contamination, and point-supervision of a single link is insufficient for articulated robots; genuine geometric safety will require full-body collision representations and cross-architecture validation.

5	\section{Limitations}\label{sec:limitations}
6	
7	All experiments use MuJoCo simulation (SafeLIBERO, two VLA families, four pick-and-place tasks); action collapse is structurally general but untested on other benchmarks or real hardware. dfCAR assumes bimodal displacement separation (Figure~\ref{fig:displacement}), which may require task-specific calibration when less pronounced. Implementation bugs that, once identified and fixed, still resulted in negative outcomes — confirming the method-level failure is not caused by engineering errors. The bug discovery→fix→re-eval narrative demonstrates scientific rigor and builds trust in the remaining results.

A: Full-body SDF requires SDF queries at multiple points along the kinematic chain, which introduces: (a) computational cost scaling linearly with the number of monitored points, (b) the need for accurate forward kinematics within the policy network to obtain link positions, and (c) gradient conflicts when different links receive opposing repulsion directions. Our work identifies this as a promising future direction — by demonstrating that EE-only is fundamentally insufficient, we motivate the investment required for full-body approaches. However, our Claim 3 (SDF is redundant when demonstrations provide avoidance) suggests that even full-body geometric supervision may be unnecessary if the demonstration data is sufficiently rich — this is an open question we leave for future work.

### Architecture Generalization

**Q: "Does action collapse affect autoregressive VLAs (RT-2, Octo), or is it specific to diffusion-based models?"**

A: Action collapse as we observe it — near-zero actions across all timesteps — arises from diffusion denoising collapsing to a single mode near zero, a failure mode documented in flow-matching training instabilities (Dong et al., 2025). Autoregressive VLAs (RT-2, Octo) use discrete token prediction, which has different failure modes (e.g., repeating stop tokens) but could produce analogous inaction artifacts. We tested Pi0 (flow matching), Pi0.5 (flow matching with language-conditioned pretraining), and confirmed OpenVLA (autoregressive) also exhibits near-zero TSR on SafeLIBERO, though we did not conduct the full dfCAR displacement analysis on OpenVLA. The dfCAR metric itself is architecture-agnostic — it filters on EE displacement regardless of how actions are generated — and we recommend its adoption for any VLA evaluation pipeline. Whether autoregressive VLAs exhibit the same bimodal displacement pattern is an empirical question we flag as future work.

### Demonstration Curation Practicality

**Q: "How practical is curating collision-free demos? Doesn't it require the same geometric knowledge as SDF?"**

A: There is a fundamental cost asymmetry. Collision-free demonstration curation is an *offline, one-time* process: a human operator or automated filter labels demonstrations as collision-free or not, requiring only binary contact detection (e.g., force sensor threshold, visual inspection, or simulator collision flag). This is available in most data collection pipelines at near-zero marginal cost. In contrast, SDF auxiliary loss requires *online, per-step* computation: at every training step, the policy must query a pre-computed SDF field, compute the signed distance for the current EE position, and backpropagate through the SDF gradient — adding both computational overhead and a dependency on accurate obstacle geometry at training time. Our Claim 3 shows the offline curation alone accounts for ~26pp CAR improvement, while the online SDF computation adds no statistically significant benefit. Practitioners should invest in demonstration quality, not geometric loss engineering.

### dfCAR Bimodal Assumption

**Q: "What if the bimodal displacement distribution doesn't hold for other robots/tasks?"**

A: The bimodality arises from task structure, not simulator specifics: manipulation tasks produce either contact-level displacement (<0.1mm, robot frozen or barely moving) or task-completion-level displacement (>100mm, robot actively reaching and grasping). This dichotomy is inherent to pick-and-place — either the robot reaches the object or it does not. We expect similar bimodality in any task with discrete contact events. That said, continuous-contact tasks (e.g., wiping, polishing) may produce a unimodal or multi-modal displacement distribution where the threshold τ_d requires task-specific calibration. We acknowledge this as an explicit limitation in the paper. Importantly, dfCAR's threshold robustness across five orders of magnitude ([2mm, 200mm]) in our experiments suggests that when bimodality exists, the exact threshold choice is not critical — the separation is structural, not marginal.

136	
137	**Q: "Action collapse is a well-known problem — what's new about your analysis?"**
138	
139	A: While action collapse has been noted anecdotally, to our knowledge, no prior work has quantified action collapse's impact on safety metrics at the scale tested here. We show that in Pi0 fine-tuned models (both full-FT and LoRA), 99.4% of episodes classified as "collision-free" exhibit obstacle displacement <0.1mm (median ~5nm) — the robot is frozen, not safe. This inflates CAR from a true ~0.5% to a reported 82–91.5%. Our contribution is (a) demonstrating the magnitude of metric contamination (80+ percentage points of CAR inflation), (b) proposing EE displacement-filtered CAR (dfCAR) as a principled correction, and (c) showing dfCAR is robust to threshold choice (δ∈[2mm, 200mm] produces identical results due to the bimodal displacement distribution: either <0.1mm or >239mm).

142	
143	A: Exactly — and that is precisely the point. Pi0 (TSR≈0%, CAR=82%) appears "safer" only because it is too broken to move. The anti-correlation between capability and apparent safety is a direct consequence of CAR conflating "unable to collide" with "able to avoid."
